question: What does NASA describe about astronaut exercise and fitness?
answer:
The most relevant passages from the curated documents are quoted below, unedited.

“Six to seven days a week, astronauts on the International Space Station perform resistance training and aerobic exercises for 1.5 hours per day to maintain their fitness and protect against muscle and bone loss. Crew members also undergo periodic fitness self-evaluations to help researchers monitor their health and fitness and to optimize the astronauts’ training regimen. Spacecraft set to carry astronauts to the Moon and Mars, however, will likely have less space for exercise equipment. Consequently, researchers are working to understand how to optimize both exercise machines and protocols to ensure that astronaut health is maintained on these deep space missions.” — Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

“Exercise training during the National Aeronautics and Space Administration 70-d bed rest study effectively counteracted the decline in aerobic capacity, muscle mass, strength, and endurance. We aimed to characterize the genomic response of the participants' vastus lateralis on day 64 of bed rest with and without exercise countermeasures. Twenty-two healthy young males were randomized into three groups: 1) bed rest only (n equals 7), 2) bed rest + aerobic (6 d/wk) and resistance training (3 d/wk) on standard equipment (n equals 7), and 3) bed rest + aerobic and resistance training using a flywheel device (n equals 8). The vastus lateralis gene and microRNA microarrays were analyzed using GeneSpring GX 14.9.1 (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA). This study hosts the microRNA microarray dataset. Gene expression microarray datasets are available in OSD-942.” — Exercise Training Attenuates the Muscle Mitochondria Genomic Response to Bed Rest (miRNA microarray data)

question: How can isolation and confinement affect crew performance?
answer:
The most relevant passages from the curated documents are quoted below, unedited.

“Selecting a crew that works well together is essential for mission success and safety. Researchers are studying how to help teams in prolonged isolation and confinement function efficiently and quickly recover after setbacks occur. They’re also mapping the myriad risks from miscommunications and related team tensions.” — Risks of Human Spaceflight

“On Earth, we have the luxury of picking up our cell phones and instantly being connected with nearly everything and everyone around us. On a trip to Mars, astronauts will be more isolated and confined than we can imagine. Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload compound this issue and may lead to decreased performance, adverse health outcomes, and compromised mission objectives. To address this hazard, experts are developing methods for monitoring behavioral health and adapting/refining various tools and technologies for use in the spaceflight environment to detect and treat early risk factors. Research is also being conducted in workload and performance, light therapy for circadian alignment, phase shifting and alertness.” — Hazard: Isolation and Confinement

question: What stressors are associated with inadequate sleep and irregular schedules?
answer:
The most relevant passages from the curated documents are quoted below, unedited.

“Space crews experience multiple hazards simultaneously. Stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands, and irregularities in their internal biological clocks. Understanding how to reduce the effects of these stressors on crew health and safety is an ongoing area of research.” — Risks of Human Spaceflight

question: What kinds of datasets does OSDR hold?
answer:
The most relevant passages from the curated documents are quoted below, unedited.

“The NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) holds multi-modal, multi-hierarchical space life science data: omics, phenotypic, physiological, behavioral, biomedical, bioimaging, environmental telemetry, hardware; tabular, text, code, imaging, video; raw and processed; from humans, animals, model organisms, tissue chips, plants, and microbes. These data and metadata support reuse for fundamental biology, applied science, and operational outcomes across space exploration and discovery.” — About OSDR
